fields.title: Vetka: test is up 6% on day three
fields.summary: Management wants to roll out today. Decide what you will do.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do with the test, and what will you propose for the quarterly plan?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Vetka.
fields.brief/company: Vetka is a fictional subscription ebook reading app: 400 thousand monthly active users, subscription after a seven-day free trial.
fields.brief/context: A test of a reminder to finish reading a book is running. On day three of the planned fourteen, variant B is ahead of the control by 6% in app opens. The Head of Growth suggests rolling out today and moving on to the next hypothesis.
fields.brief/objective: Decide what to do with the test and the quarterly plan.
fields.brief/constraints: One team, three to four experiments per quarter. The quarterly plan is defended in two weeks.
fields.brief/task: Choose what to do and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Conditions are set before the start — otherwise it is not a test
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A metric, a timeline, and a minimum detectable effect set in advance are the only things that distinguish an experiment from hunting for a nice number. Intermediate results are almost always inflated, and weekends or external events explain them better than your hypothesis. The result should be recorded along with what it does not prove: otherwise, the company tests the same thing over and over in circles.
fields.evidenceCards/0/title: What is known about the test itself
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Hypothesis: a reminder about an unfinished book will bring people back to reading, because they drop off on chapter two or three.

Primary metric set before start: share of users who finish their first book. Timeline: 14 days. Minimum detectable effect: 3%.

On day three: app opens +6%, finished first book +0.9% (within noise).

Test running since Friday. Day three is Sunday.

On Monday, a high-profile new release came out that was covered by all book channels.

Guardrail metrics: notification unsubscribes +14%, support complaints unchanged.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Experiment records are kept in a shared spreadsheet, but it is updated irregularly: 11 records in a year out of about 20 conducted tests.

A year ago, personalized recommendations on the main screen were tested: started books +0.4% (insignificant), finished books −2%. Card conclusion: "the problem is not in book choice, but in dropping an already started book".

Six months ago, a daily notification "time to read" was tested: opens +9% in week one, after a month the effect disappeared, notification unsubscribes grew by 22%. No record exists for this — only one developer remembers it.

At a meeting, someone suggested returning to personalized recommendations: "we didn't seem to finish that".
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
A. Personalized recommendations on the main screen. Reach 400k, medium effect estimate, low confidence, 6 weeks test.

B. Short reading goal ("20 pages a day"). Reach 180k active readers, medium effect, medium confidence (in interviews 12 people mentioned dropping off without a routine), 2 weeks test.

C. Remove registration before the trial period. Reach 90k new users per month, high effect, high confidence (funnel shows 38% lost at registration), 2 weeks test.

D. Dark mode for reader. Reach 400k, low effect, full confidence, 3 weeks test.

E. Audio versions — request from Commercial Director, estimate 4 months, cannot be tested cheaply.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What is expected from the quarterly plan
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Sales asks for a six-month feature roadmap with dates: they need something to show partners.

Commercial Director wants audiobooks in the plan for this quarter.

The previous quarterly plan was a list of seven features with dates. Three were completed, two canceled after initial data, two postponed.

Since then, people repeat at meetings: "product never delivers what it promised".

Half-year goal agreed with management: raise share of users who finish their first book from 31% to 40%. It directly links to subscription renewal: users finishing their first book renew 2.3 times more often.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Run the test to completion and build a problem-focused plan
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Do not stop the test early, focus on the predefined metric, record the result alongside past ones, and build the quarterly plan around the completion goal.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
You show the Head of Growth three things: the primary metric is completion, not opens; day three coincided with a weekend and a major book release; notification unsubscribes are already at +14%. He agrees to wait.
By day fourteen, the completion effect is +1.2% — positive, but three times lower than the minimum detectable 3%, while unsubscribes settled at +11%. You decide not to roll out.
You locate the unrecorded past test on daily notifications: it had +9% opens that faded within a month. You record both cards; a general principle about notifications in this product emerges.
In the plan, you place C (registration: 38% loss, two weeks, high confidence) and B (reading routine). You skip recommendations — the year-old card explains why, and the discussion takes ten minutes.
You present the plan by horizons: problem, metric, what we are testing. You give Sales talking points without dates.
Trade-off: audiobooks are not in the plan, and the Commercial Director remains dissatisfied.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Roll out today and move on
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: 6% is a noticeable result, waiting eleven more days is expensive. Roll out to everyone and take on the next hypothesis.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The rollout happens on Monday. Two weeks later, the opens metric returns to its baseline: the spike was due to the weekend and the new release.
The share of users finishing their first book does not move at all — nobody checked it.
Notification unsubscribes rise to +19% and stay there; the next notification test has nowhere to run — half the audience disabled them.
The 6% figure enters the quarterly plan as justification, and at the defense you have to explain where the promise came from.
Trade-off: false confidence gained and the notification channel damaged for the future; the test cannot be repeated fairly.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Extend the test and look at other metrics
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Since there is no effect on completion yet, extend the test by another two weeks and add metrics — maybe an effect will show up in retention or subscription renewal.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Extending buys time, which is better than an immediate rollout.
However, metrics were added after the start, and after a month one shows +2.8% — on subscriptions. Significance is marginal, and no one can tell whether this was promised in advance or found through p-hacking.
The decision made is controversial, and at the plan defense it looks like data fitting — rightly so.
Unsubscribes reach +17% over the month because the test ran longer.
Trade-off: timeline and metrics became fluid, so the result cannot be trusted, no matter how much data accumulates.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Focus on the plan and leave the test to the team
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The plan defense is in two weeks, which is more important. Build a horizon roadmap around the completion goal, and let the test run its course.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The plan turns out well: problems instead of features, goal 31% → 40%, hypotheses ranked, C and B at the top. Sales gets a clear frame, and you explain to the Commercial Director why audiobooks do not fit.
However, without you, the test is stopped on day five based on the same 6% opens — the team considered it obvious.
A line appears in the plan: "reminders work, +6%", and the next two experiments are built on it.
A month later, it turns out there is no effect, and part of the plan has to be rebuilt.
Trade-off: correct work done in one place while leaving unsupervised the source of numbers that work relies on.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Hypotheses are compared by appeal rather than reach, effect, and testing cost
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Experiment conditions are set after seeing the numbers
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The result is not converted into documented knowledge with boundaries of inference
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The roadmap looks like a list of features with dates instead of problems and metrics
